raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male patient presented with high-grade continuous fever, headache, vomiting for 8 days, severe headache and vomiting for 4 days, and altered sensorium for 1-day. There was no history of convulsion during this period.
On neurological examination, he had neck rigidity with positive Kernig sign. GCS Score was E2M4V1. No cranial nerve abnormality was noted. Plantar was nonresponsive bilaterally, and hypotonia was found in all four limbs. Power could not be tested.
MRI scan of brain done on 9th day of fever showed areas of hyperintensities involving bilateral periventricular and parietal region with signal changes involving right cerebellar peduncle with involvement of upper brainstem which were suggestive of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) [Figure 7].
Patient became fully conscious after 2 days. Then on motor system examination it was revealed that he had quadriparesis with the power of right lower extremity 1/5, left lower extremity 2/5, and both right and left upper extremity 4/5. All deep tendon reflexes were diminished. There was no sensory impairment. MRI of whole spine showed hyperintense intramedullary signal changes involving spinal cord extending from C3 level downward until conus suggestive of myelitis with cord edema [Figure 7]. CSF study showed immunoglobulin synthesis index 0.72, immunoglobulin synthesis rate 6.5 mg/day with no oligoclonal bands. VEP was also normal. Autoimmune markers such as ANA, pANCA, and cANCA were negative.
So, a revised diagnosis of dengue meningoencephalomyelitis was made, and he was put on IV methylprednisolone 1 g once daily for 5 days. Patient regained his power in upper extremities, but both lower extremities had 4/5 power on discharge. At first follow-up, after 3 weeks of discharge he had no residual paraparesis.
Both the patient presented with fever (for 7 and 8 days), headache (both for 5 days), recurrent episode of vomiting (for 2 days and 1-day), and disorientation (both for 1-day). One had purpuric spots in lower extremities for 1-day. They had impaired sensorium on admission (GCS 8 and 9) but unremarkable neurological examination except for abnormal plantar response (B/L extensor and nonresponsive). One patient had severe hyponatremia, and other one had hyponatremia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Both the patients had elevated transaminase level. Both the patients had normal MRI brain and normal CSF picture. Both the patients regained their sensorium after conservative management and electrolyte correction within 7 days. So, metabolic abnormalities caused by dengue virus were considered as the cause for the CNS manifestations in both the patients and diagnosed as dengue encephalopathy. Both of them were discharged at the end of 2nd week.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presented with an 8-day history of continuous high-grade fever, headache, and vomiting (worsening over 4 days) and 1 day of altered sensorium, alongside two additional patients presenting with 7-8 days of fever, 5 days of headache, vomiting, and 1 day of disorientation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The primary 19-year-old patient developed 8 days of continuous high-grade fever, headache, and vomiting (severe for 4 days) and 1 day of altered sensorium without seizures; after regaining consciousness on hospital day 2, he was found to have asymmetric quadriparesis. Two additional patients in the series presented with 7 and 8 days of fever, 5 days of headache, 1-2 days of recurrent vomiting, and 1 day of disorientation (one with lower-limb purpura).
subjective.review_of_systems: Primary patient: continuous high-grade fever, severe headache, vomiting, altered sensorium, and quadriparesis (no convulsions). Additional two patients: fever (7-8 days), headache (5 days), recurrent vomiting, disorientation, and lower-limb purpuric spots in one patient.

objective.physical_examination: Primary patient: admission GCS E2M4V1, neck rigidity, positive Kernig sign, intact cranial nerves, nonresponsive plantar reflexes, and four-limb hypotonia; on day 2 (conscious), exhibited quadriparesis (right lower limb 1/5, left lower limb 2/5, bilateral upper limbs 4/5) and diminished deep tendon reflexes with intact sensation. Two additional patients: admission GCS 8 and 9, purpuric lower-extremity spots in one, and abnormal plantar responses (bilateral extensor and nonresponsive) with otherwise unremarkable neurological exams.
objective.routine_investigations: Primary patient: normal visual evoked potentials (VEP) and negative ANA, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA. Two additional encephalopathy patients: elevated transaminases in both, severe hyponatremia in one, and hyponatremia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia in the other.
objective.advanced_workup: Primary patient: day-9 brain MRI showed hyperintensities in the bilateral periventricular and parietal white matter, right cerebellar peduncle, and upper brainstem (ADEM-like); whole-spine MRI showed longitudinally extensive intramedullary T2 hyperintensity and cord edema from C3 to the conus medullaris; CSF showed immunoglobulin synthesis index 0.72, Ig synthesis rate 6.5 mg/day, and no oligoclonal bands. Two additional patients: normal brain MRI and normal CSF analysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary patient: Dengue meningoencephalomyelitis (post-dengue ADEM with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis from C3 to conus), treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, achieving full upper-limb recovery and 4/5 lower-limb strength at discharge and complete resolution of paraparesis at 3-week follow-up. Two additional patients: Metabolic dengue encephalopathy (secondary to hyponatremia and hepatic dysfunction with normal brain MRI/CSF), managed conservatively with fluid and electrolyte correction with full recovery of sensorium within 7 days and discharge at 2 weeks.
